quotes.text: Sea Scrolls, we learn that it was Pharaoh that gave Abraham Hagar. We are also told that Lot took a wife from the "daughters of Egypt." Question: What is the law of Sarah? The law of Sarah is that she gives her husband another wife. Depending on how you read the Pearl of Great Price, and Genesis, Sarah appears to be at least 50 at this time. But they lived longer in those days. Abraham lived to be 175. Now let's get to the meat of Abraham. Here is a man who is promised a posterity forever, and a land, and he has neither. That is pretty strange. How did it make him look? You go around saying that you have a deal with the only God that exists, that you will have a lot of kids, and lands, and you have neither. He is surrounded by kings with many sons and daughters, and lands. What is going on here. How many times does the Lord tell him and reconfirm the covenant with him. He reconfirms it numerous times, as Abraham gets older and older. His actual election apparently does not occur until the sacrifice of Isaac. At that point he gets a new name; until then, the Lord has reviewed with him the covenant, and reconfirmed it, from several points of view. Recall the Pearl of Great Price, with the Urim and Thummim, and he sees the entire universe, and God tells him that his seed will be as numerous as the stars he sees. He further shows him that the way the universe is set up, it is the same way the Lord has his children set up. Why not. Everything is made to bear record of the Son of God. The universe is the basic pattern of everything he does.

quotes.text: Holy women The Lord never sends apostles and prophets and righteous men to minister to his people without placing women of like spiritual stature at their sides. Adam stands as the great high priest, under Christ, to rule as a natural patriarch over all men of all ages, but he cannot rule alone; Eve, his wife, rules at his side, having like caliber and attainments to his own. Abraham is tested as few men have been when the Lord commands him to offer Isaac upon the altar (Gen. 22:1-19); and Sarah struggles with like problems when the Lord directs that she withhold from the Egyptians her status as Abraham's wife. (Abra. 2:21-25; Gen. 12:7-20.) Isaac gains from the Lord the promise that his seed shall "multiply as the stars of heaven" (Gen. 26:1-4); and Rebekah, his wife, receives a blessing of her own in which she is promised that she shall be "the mother of thousands of millions." (Gen. 24:59-60.) And so it goes, in all dispensations and at all times when there are holy men there are also holy women. Neither stands alone before the Lord. The exaltation of the one is dependent upon that of the other.

notes.text: "The thrice repeated story [involving Abraham in 12:10-20 and 20:1-18, and Isaac in 26:6-12] has been the subject of much discussion by commentators through the ages, but only with the discoveries at Nuzi has it become clear that Abraham and Isaac were not involved in any trickery, but were endeavoring to protect their respective wives from molestation by invoking the Hurrian custom or law of wife-sistership. According to the Nuzi tablets a woman having the status of wife-sister rather than that of just an ordinary wife, enjoyed superior privileges and was better protected. The status was a purely legal one, a wife-sister being quite distinct from the physical relationship usually understood by the word 'sister.' In order to create the status of wife-sistership two documents were prepared-one for marriage and the other for sistership. Thus, we find a Nuzi tablet, according to which a person by the name of Akkuleni, son of Akiya, contracted with one Hurazzi, son of Eggaya, to give to Hurazzi in marriage his sister Beltakkadummi. Another tablet records that the same Akkuleni sold his sister Beltakkadummi as sister to the same Hurazzi. If such a marriage was violated, the punishment was much more severe than in the case of a straightforward ordinary marriage. It would appear that the actions of Abraham and Isaac reflect this custom." (Stuart A. West, "The Nuzi Tablets." Bible and Spade 10:3-4 (Summer-Autumn 1981):67. See also E. A. Speiser. Anchor Bible series, no. 1. Garden City, N.Y.: Doubleday, 1964, pp. 91-92.)

sister ('achowth) beloved bride - wife of the covenant. Ancient documents indicate that there were three orders or classes of wives in the Old Testament. The first was concubine, piylegesh. This was a woman who entered into marriage without the usual ceremony. The second order, the most common one, was 'ishshah. This woman entered into marriage with the customary ceremony. The third order was 'achowth. She entered into special marriage covenants which are not detailed in the written text. The 'ishshah order of wife had very few legal rights in comparison with her husband. The 'achowth, the covenant wife, on the other hand, had full legal rights. She fully participated in all of the blessings of the marriage bond. Abraham used the word, 'achowth, as he warned Pharaoh about his special relationship to Sarah. One can make a case that in the Hebrew text that Abraham informed Pharaoh about his eternal marriage covenants with Sarah. These covenants made her a sister in the covenant and Pharaoh would do well in leaving her alone. Pharaoh fails to heed Abraham's warning and is cursed. The Lord only curses people when there has been a violation of divine law.

It was not until the discovery of ancient Hurrian legal texts at the site of Nuzi, a city east of Ashur, the capital of ancient Assyria, that we obtained a clearer background for this incident. The Hurrians were people who flourished about the time of Abraham, and later. Their kingdom included the land of Haran in which Abraham and Sarah lived for a number of years before moving to Canaan (Genesis 11:31). There are three levels of wife in the ancient world. According to EA Speiser, in Genesis Anchor Bible Commentary, notes that in some ancient societies that the husband did not only marry the wife but adopted her as his sister. This was the highest form of marriage. The wife at that point had the highest of all legal rights. Three levels of wife are: concubine (piylegesh) wife ('ishshah)\ sister ('achowth)
